{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"interview-synthesis-round1","url":"https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec8154830ec820ca375e6e","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec8154830ec820ca375e6e as of 2026-04-27T03:26:19.047Z: {"title":"interview-synthesis-round1"} # Acme — Interview Synthesis: Round 1 **Period:** August–September 2025 **Interviews conducted:** 8 **Format:** 45-min Zoom, using interview guide v1.0 **Synthesized by:** Bryan Chen (CEO) + Sarah Kim (Head of Product) **Date of synthesis:** October 1, 2025 **Status:** Final --- ## Participant Overview
Pseudonym Company Stage Team Size EM Experience HR Support?
Tyler R. Series A 8 reports 3 years None
Patrick M. Series B 12 reports 6 years HRBP (part-time)
Alison B. Series B 6 reports 2 years None
David K. Series A 5 reports 1.5 years None
Priya S. Seed 4 reports 1 year None
Jason L. Series B 14 reports 8 years Full HRBP
Michelle T. Series A 7 reports 2 years None
Raj N. Series C 18 reports 5 years Full HRBP
--- ## Method Note All 8 interviews were conducted using guide v1.0. We focused primarily on problem exploration; none of the participants were shown a product (we were pre-prototype at this point). Quotes have been lightly edited for clarity. Names are pseudonyms. --- ## Theme 1: Meeting load is the primary complaint, but it’s a proxy for something deeper Every participant mentioned being in too many meetings. But when we probed further, the issue wasn’t meetings per se — it was the loss of thinking time that comes from constant context-switching. Tyler R.: *“I have 22 recurring meetings on my calendar and that’s before anything urgent gets added. By Thursday I’m just reacting. There’s no time to actually think about how my people are doing.”* Patrick M.: *“The calendar is full, but that’s not really the problem. The problem is that by the time I get to a 1:1, I haven’t had a minute to think about what I actually want to accomplish. So I just ask how things are going and we talk about tickets.”* **Insight:** EMs aren’t asking us to reduce their meetings. They’re asking us to help them use the time they have more intentionally. The 1:1 is the canonical example — it exists in the calendar, but most participants admitted the quality was low because of lack of preparation. **Implication:** The “preparation” use case is more concrete and more urgent than we originally thought. We should focus there first. --- ## Theme 2: Preparation happens in scattered, fragmented ways When asked how they prep for 1:1s, 6 of 8 participants described a version of the same workflow: scrolling through Slack, glancing at Jira/Linear, and trying to remember what was discussed last week. Alison B.: *“I have a Notion page for each person and I try to keep notes there, but honestly I only update it like half the time. So I’m relying on Slack search most of the time. It’s not great.”* David K.: *“I don’t really prep. I know I should. I just run out of time and then I’m in the meeting and I’m asking questions I probably already know the answers to.”* Michelle T.: *“I have a shared doc with each person where they add their agenda items, but I’m not always sure what happened since the last conversation. I have to piece it together.”* **Insight:** The absence of a structured, maintained record of 1:1 history is a universal pain point. But interestingly, most participants have tried to solve it with Notion or Google Docs and partially abandoned it — not because the concept is wrong, but because the maintenance overhead is too high. **Implication:** Any solution we build must have low friction to maintain. The product has to do the work of capturing and organizing — not ask the manager to be more disciplined. --- ## Theme 3: Performance reviews are dreaded, not because of the feedback, but because of the recall problem 6 of 8 participants described the performance review process as significantly more stressful than it should be, and for the same reason: they couldn’t confidently reconstruct 6 months of context. Tyler R.: *“The review template asks me to provide specific examples of impact. And I know the work was good, but I’m trying to remember something specific from April and I just… can’t. So I write something vague and it sounds thin and I know it.”* Patrick M.: *“I’ve gotten better over the years at keeping notes, but it’s still a scramble. I’ll spend 4 hours per person. For 12 people, that’s two full work days that I’m basically just trying to remember things.”* Jason L. (with HRBP support): *“Even with HR support, the information I need to write a good review is all in my head. The HRBP helps with the process, but not with the content.”* **Insight:** The performance review problem is not fundamentally about the review — it’s about the absence of longitudinal, structured data about each report. If that data existed and was easy to access, the review would write itself. **Implication:** This is the long-term value case for Acme. The 1:1 product is the front door; the performance review use case is what makes the product irreplaceable after 3–6 months of use. --- ## Theme 4: Career development is where the guilt lives This theme was not in our original research plan but emerged unprompted across 5 of 8 interviews. Participants felt most guilty about not doing enough around career development — not just performance management. Michelle T.: *“I know I’m supposed to be doing career development conversations. I do them maybe once a quarter. And even then I feel like I’m just checking a box rather than actually helping them go somewhere.”* Alison B.: *“I’m a newer manager. I don’t feel confident enough in my own career trajectory to give advice about someone else’s. I want a way to be more structured about it without it feeling like I’m making it up.”* Priya S.: *“My most senior engineer is going to want to talk about the staff engineer track. I have no idea how to have that conversation in a meaningful way. I keep putting it off.”* **Insight:** Career development is a high-anxiety, low-frequency activity for most EMs in our target segment. They lack both the time and the frameworks to do it well. This is an underexplored area for our product — and likely one where AI assistance would feel most valuable, because the “right answer” varies so much by person. **Implication:** Add career development framing to the product vision. Not as a v1 feature, but as a directional signal for where the product should go. --- ## Theme 5: Tooling skepticism is real but surmountable 3 of 8 participants expressed some version of “I’ve tried tools before and they didn’t stick.” The pattern: purchase Lattice or 15Five, use it for 30–60 days, abandon it because it required too much manual data entry or felt too HR-facing rather than manager-facing. Tyler R.: *“We had Lattice. I filled in the forms when I had to. I never looked at it again. It felt like reporting to HR, not a tool for me.”* Jason L.: *“15Five is okay for the check-in habit. But it doesn’t connect to anything. I still have to go from 15Five to Jira to GitHub to try to piece together what’s actually happening.”* **Insight:** The existing tools in this space are perceived as administrative, compliance-oriented, and manager-unfriendly. The managers who tried them and abandoned them are not resistant to tooling — they’re resistant to tools that don’t actually reduce their workload. This is our primary positioning opportunity. **Implication:** Our go-to-market messaging should lean into this explicitly: “Built for the manager, not for HR.” --- ## Surprising / Disconfirming Data **Surprising:** Two participants (Jason L. and Raj N.) had HRBP support and still expressed the same core pain around recall and preparation. We had assumed HRBP access would reduce the pain — it doesn’t, because the data problem is personal to the manager, not something an HRBP can solve. **Disconfirming:** We hypothesized that EMs primarily wanted better team analytics (velocity, PR metrics, etc.). Only 2 of 8 participants brought up quantitative team metrics unprompted. The dominant need is qualitative — conversation history, career context, personal signals. The “data” EMs need most is not the data from their dev tools. --- ## Segment Differences
Factor Finding
**Smaller teams (\<8)** More likely to wing it; preparation habits less established; pain is real but urgency is lower
**Larger teams (12+)** Preparation and recall pain is most acute; most likely to pay for a solution
**\<2 years experience** Career development anxiety is highest; most likely to want frameworks and guidance
**5+ years experience** More opinionated about workflow; more resistant to tools that add process; interested in automation
--- ## Recommended Actions 1. **Define the MVP around 1:1 preparation and continuity.** This is the most universal, most immediately painful problem. Build from here. 2. **Make the data capture invisible.** Any solution that requires manual note entry will be abandoned. Design for passive capture. 3. **Explicitly position against HR tools.** The frame of “this is yours, not HR’s” is our strongest differentiator from Lattice/15Five. 4. **Add career development to the long-term roadmap.** Not v1, but don’t design v1 in a way that makes it impossible to add later. 5. **Conduct 3–4 follow-up sessions specifically on the performance review problem.** We have directional signal but not enough behavioral depth yet. --- ## Open Questions - How do we design for passive capture without requiring deep integrations that create implementation friction? - What’s the right model for data ownership and privacy? EMs are nervous about anything that feels surveillance-adjacent. - Is there a team-size below which the pain isn’t acute enough to convert to paying? (Hypothesis: \<5 direct reports is too small) --- *Next research round planned for November 2025. Focus: prototype feedback and performance review deep dive.* "}

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"prd-v2-insights-dashboard","url":"https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec8177bd3ce4bf2ca797a1","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec8177bd3ce4bf2ca797a1 as of 2026-04-27T03:26:20.150Z: {"title":"prd-v2-insights-dashboard"} # PRD: Manager Insights Dashboard — v2.0 **Status:** In Development (target GA: April 2026) **Feature:** Team health dashboard + performance review drafting assist **Product Owner:** Sarah Kim **Engineering Lead:** Marcus Webb **Design:** Marcus Webb **Stakeholders:** Bryan Chen (CEO) **Last Updated:** February 2026 --- ## Background & Context Acme v1 shipped the 1:1 Assistant in November 2025. As of February 2026, we have 47 Weekly Active Managers and have conducted two rounds of post-launch user research. The core value loop — take structured notes → see history → feel more prepared — is working for our most engaged users. The pattern we’re seeing: users who get through weeks 1–3 and establish a note-taking habit become highly retained. The challenge is that weeks 1–3 are fragile. The product’s long-term value (longitudinal history, AI suggestions based on accumulated context) is not yet accessible to new users, creating an “investment before return” dynamic that is driving early churn. This PRD defines the v2.0 feature set, which addresses two things simultaneously:
1. **Dashboard:** Give users a reason to open Acme even when a 1:1 isn’t happening — something with ambient, daily value.
2. **Performance Review Drafting:** Unlock the most-anticipated long-term use case using the data that’s now accumulating. --- ## Problem Statements ### Problem 1: No reason to open the product between 1:1s The v1 product is session-triggered. Users only get value when they’re actively in or preparing for a 1:1. This means the product is invisible 5–6 days of the week, which makes habit formation slow and churn risk high. **Desired state:** Managers come to Acme proactively, not just reactively. ### Problem 2: The performance review payoff is abstract until it’s real One of our biggest acquisition messages is “stop scrambling at review time.” But new users can’t experience this until they’ve been using the product for 3–6 months. We need to make this payoff more tangible, sooner. **Desired state:** A user can draft a meaningful performance summary after 6+ weeks of note-taking — not a full review write-up, but a solid starting point. --- ## Goals **Dashboard:**
- Increase days-per-week active (currently 1.3 avg; target 2.5 by 90 days post-launch)
- Increase % of users who open Acme on a day without a 1:1 (currently \~12%; target 35%) **Performance Review Drafting:**
- 80% of users who have 6+ weeks of note history attempt the drafting feature within 2 weeks of GA
- 65% of those users rate the output as “useful” or “very useful” on exit survey **Retention:**
- Reduce 30-day churn from 28% to under 18% --- ## Non-Goals - Real-time Slack or GitHub integrations (remains future scope — see integration PRD) - Manager-of-manager org-level views (future scope) - Formal HR workflows (calibrations, ratings submission, etc.) - Full performance review automation (we are generating a *draft* — the manager writes the final version) --- ## Feature 1: Manager Insights Dashboard ### Overview A lightweight, glanceable home screen that surfaces what’s happening across the manager’s team. Not a surveillance tool — a preparation tool. The frame is: “what do I need to be thinking about this week?” ### Components **Weekly overview card**
- Which 1:1s are scheduled this week
- Which reports have open action items that are overdue
- Which reports haven’t had a 1:1 in 3+ weeks (at-risk flag) **Action item inbox**
- All open action items across all reports, sorted by due date
- One-click to mark done or snooze
- This is the primary “daily reason to open” — the manager can do a 5-minute action-item review without opening a specific session **Report health snapshot (per person)**
- Last 1:1 date
- Count of open action items (manager + report)
- Trend indicator: note volume trending up or down over the past 4 sessions
- (Note: no AI-generated “health score” in v2 — we will not claim to know if someone is at risk without better data) **Upcoming 1:1 prep nudge**
- For any 1:1 scheduled in the next 24 hours, surface a “prepare” button
- Opens the session view pre-loaded with last 3 sessions and open action items
- Optional: brief AI-generated prep note (“You have 2 open action items with Priya and haven’t discussed career growth in 6 weeks”) ### Design Decisions **Decision:** No numerical scores or ratings on the health snapshot **Rationale:** Scores create false precision and risk being misused (e.g., “Priya’s health score is 3.2”). We’re not building a surveillance tool. The goal is to surface what the manager already knows but can’t easily see, not to generate new judgments about people. **Decision:** Action item inbox is the primary use case for between-1:1 engagement **Rationale:** Round 2 research showed action item tracking was the most emotionally resonant feature of v1. It’s also the most concrete daily task — managers can do a 2-minute action item review with real outcomes. --- ## Feature 2: Performance Review Drafting Assist ### Overview For managers who have 6+ weeks of note history in Acme, a performance review drafting tool that generates a structured starting point — not a finished review, but a first draft that compresses the recall work the manager would otherwise have to do. ### User Flow **Entry point:** From a report’s profile, a “Draft performance summary” button appears once the report has 6+ weeks of session history. **Step 1 — Set the period**
Manager specifies the review period (e.g., “Q4 2025, October–December”). **Step 2 — Review the source material**
Before generating anything, the product shows the manager what notes will be used. This is a trust-building moment: the manager can see we’re working from their actual content, not making things up. They can exclude specific sessions from the draft. **Step 3 — Draft generation**
AI generates a structured draft with the following sections:
- **Achievements:** Specific wins mentioned or discussed in sessions, with approximate timeframes
- **Growth areas:** Recurring themes that the manager identified as development opportunities
- **Action items summary:** Major commitments that were made and resolved
- **Open goals:** Anything stated as a goal that hasn’t been marked resolved **Step 4 — Edit and finalize**
Inline editing of the draft. The manager owns the final output. Acme makes no assumptions about ratings, levels, or calibration context. **Step 5 — Export**
Copy to clipboard or export as plain text. The output is designed to drop into whatever performance management tool the company uses. ### What the Draft Does NOT Include - Ratings or numerical assessments — we have no context on the company’s rating framework - Comparison to peers — we only have data on this one person - Compensation recommendations - Anything inferred from data sources we don’t have (e.g., PR merge rate, code quality) ### AI Approach The AI prompt is structured to work from the manager’s exact note content. We do not allow the AI to synthesize beyond what’s in the notes — if a note says “Marcus is struggling with prioritization,” the draft can say “Prioritization was identified as a development area.” It cannot say “Marcus may not be meeting the expectations of the role.” We will disclose to the user that the output is AI-generated and should be edited before submission. --- ## Revised Session-Start Experience (addressing Round 2 feedback) This is technically a bug fix / UX improvement, but it belongs in this PRD because it unblocks adoption of all v2 features. **Current state:** Users navigate to the report profile, then click “New session,” then begin the session. This requires 2–3 clicks from the home screen. **v2 state:**
- From the dashboard, tapping a report’s name while they have a 1:1 today goes directly into session view
- New “quick capture” keyboard shortcut: `Cmd+K` opens a modal where the manager can select a report and begin typing — no navigation required
- Session auto-saves and files itself to the correct report --- ## Privacy Model — Explicit Onboarding Statement This should be built as a product feature, not just a terms of service item. **On first login, display:** > **Your notes are yours.** Everything you write in Acme is private to you. Your employer cannot access your notes, your session history, or your action items. If you leave your company, your data stays with your account. We use your note content to generate suggestions and summaries — all processing happens in Acme. We do not share your note content with your employer, your HR team, or any third parties. \[I understand — let’s get started\] This is a one-time prompt at first login. It should be revisitable in Settings. --- ## Metrics & Instrumentation Events to log (new in v2):
Event Description
`dashboard_opened` User opens the dashboard home
`action_item_resolved` User marks an action item done from the dashboard
`1on1_prep_clicked` User clicks “prepare” on an upcoming 1:1
`draft_initiated` User begins a performance review draft
`draft_completed` User completes and exports a draft
`draft_quality_rating` User rates the draft quality (1–5, prompted on export)
`session_started_quick_capture` User starts a session via `Cmd+K`
--- ## Open Questions 1. **When should we send a weekly summary email?** The dashboard is pull-based; we need a push mechanism to re-engage users who don’t open the product organically. A Monday morning summary email showing the week’s 1:1s and open action items is the obvious candidate. Need to validate that users want this vs. perceive it as noise. 2. **What’s the right minimum history for the draft feature?** We’ve said 6 weeks, but this is a guess. We should test whether drafts generated from 4 weeks of notes are useful. Lower threshold = more users unlock the feature sooner = faster retention payoff. 3. **Should we let managers see their own notes from past reports (people who have left the team)?** Useful for longitudinal learning; could raise privacy concerns from the report’s perspective. Defer to post-GA. --- ## Dependencies - Auth system must support data-portability model (user owns data, not org) - AI model API (current: Anthropic Claude, via API) — no change to provider needed - Note storage schema — requires migration from v1 to support session-level inclusion/exclusion in drafts --- ## Launch Plan **Internal dog food:** Week of March 9, 2026 — Bryan and Sarah test dashboard + draft feature on real data **Beta:** March 23 — Invite top 20 WAMs from existing user base **GA:** April 13, 2026 — All users, no waitlist --- ## Success Review Date June 1, 2026 — Full review of dashboard engagement and draft quality metrics. Decision point: do we invest further in the performance review use case or pivot toward team-level analytics? "}

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"product-iteration-learnings","url":"https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec81cea8aed2e7c9182e78","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec81cea8aed2e7c9182e78 as of 2026-04-27T03:26:24.485Z: {"title":"product-iteration-learnings"} # Acme — Product Iteration Learnings **Document Type:** Living retrospective **Period covered:** July 2025 – March 2026 **Owner:** Bryan Chen (CEO) + Sarah Kim (Head of Product) **Last Updated:** March 2026 **Audience:** Internal team + investors --- ## Purpose This document captures the key learnings from Acme’s first 8 months of product development — what we built, why we built it, what happened, and what we’d do differently. It is deliberately candid. We’d rather document the mistakes clearly than pretend the path was straight. --- ## Phase 0: Pre-Product (July–September 2025) ### What we did We spent the first two months doing nothing but talking to engineering managers. 8 structured interviews using our v1 interview guide. No product, no prototype, no landing page — just conversations. ### What we learned **The problem is real, but the expression of it is misleading.**
Every EM we talked to said some version of “I’m too busy.” If we had taken that at face value, we might have built a meeting scheduler or a time-blocker. What we found instead, when we dug deeper, was that the real pain wasn’t time — it was *context*. Managers don’t have good recall of their people, and that drives everything downstream. **Performance reviews are the most emotionally charged pain point.**
Managers are mildly bothered by 1:1 prep. They’re genuinely ashamed by the quality of their performance reviews. That shame is strong signal. Ashamed people pay to solve the problem. **The competitive frame matters.**
When we described Acme as “like Lattice but better,” we got eye-rolls. When we described it as “the opposite of Lattice — it’s yours, not HR’s,” we got leaning forward. The distinction between a manager-side tool and an HR tool is not subtle — it’s the positioning entirely. ### What we’d do differently Start with cleaner research design. Our v1 interview guide was too feature-focused and not behavioral enough. We wasted 2–3 sessions that could have been more productive. The v2 guide is much better — we should have written it before the first session, not after the fourth. --- ## Phase 1: First Prototype (October–November 2025) ### What we built A structured 1:1 note-taking interface with session persistence, an action item tracker, and AI-generated talking point suggestions. Built in 5 weeks. Shipped to 7 beta users. ### What we got right **Persistence was immediately, viscerally valuable.**
Within one week of beta launch, we had users describing the product in the terms we hoped for: “I don’t lose context anymore.” That’s the job. We nailed it faster than expected. **Action item tracking was a surprise hit.**
We built it as a secondary feature. It became the first thing users talked about in debrief sessions. The reason: it changes how their reports experience them. It’s not just a productivity feature — it’s a credibility feature. ### What we got wrong **The session-start experience was too clunky.**
We built the UI assuming users would open the product before starting a meeting. In practice, meetings start informally and the tool needs to be there when the user remembers. Three clicks to start a session is two clicks too many. **AI suggestions landed flat.**
We over-invested in the suggestion quality before we had enough data to generate meaningful suggestions. The first month of suggestions were generic because the note history was thin. Users noticed. Their word: “generic.” We should have designed the AI feature to be invisible in week 1 and gradually surface as the data accumulates, rather than showing it prominently from day one. **We didn’t design for the first two weeks.**
The product is most valuable after 4–6 weeks of accumulated notes. But we didn’t build anything to carry users through weeks 1–2 when the return on investment is low. One user churned in week 3, explicitly citing that the product hadn’t given him enough back for what he was putting in. This was a preventable churn. ### Metrics at the end of Phase 1
Metric Target Actual
Beta users 5 7
30-day retention 70% 72%
WAW (weekly active writers) 60% 64%
Average session length ≥8 min 9.3 min
Action item usage — (not tracked) 78% of sessions
--- ## Phase 2: GA Launch & Growth (December 2025 – February 2026) ### What we built - Opened the product to a broader waitlist - Fixed 12 UX issues from beta feedback - Shipped a basic roster view - Began tracking in-product analytics seriously for the first time ### What we got right **Starting with a focused waitlist worked.**
We didn’t do a broad launch. We invited Round 1 interview participants, their referrals, and a handful of people from the Rands Leadership Slack. This gave us users who had context on the problem and were predisposed to engage seriously. WAM grew from 7 to 47 in this period, entirely through word of mouth and targeted outreach. **Referrals are our best channel.**
Every user who stayed past 30 days has referred at least one other person. The referral rate is higher than we expected and the conversion of referrals is dramatically higher than cold outreach (\~30% vs. \~8%). **Analytics unlocked real insights.**
Once we started tracking events (session_started, note_saved, action_item_created, etc.), we found patterns we hadn’t seen in interviews. Example: 65% of users open the product on Monday morning, but only 22% open it on Friday. This told us our product is being used as a “start of week planning” tool more than we realized, which has implications for the dashboard design. ### What we got wrong **We underestimated the privacy concern.**
Three users in the GA cohort asked about data privacy within their first week. Two of them were more concerned than any of our beta users. We hadn’t emphasized privacy in our GA onboarding. This was a mistake that may have cost us users who didn’t ask the question but had the concern. **We over-prioritized AI feature development.**
In December, we spent 2 weeks improving the AI suggestion algorithm. The improvement was real — suggestions got more specific. But WAM didn’t move. Users who didn’t like the suggestions still didn’t like them. The core retention issue wasn’t suggestion quality — it was the early-weeks experience. We misread the signal. **We didn’t have a good answer for the “why now” question.**
Several prospects we talked to during outreach said some version of: “This sounds useful, but I’m already managing somehow. Why would I add another tool right now?” We didn’t have a crisp response. The answer is probably “because the cost of a bad performance review is higher than you think, and it’s coming in 90 days” — but we hadn’t articulated that yet. ### Metrics at end of Phase 2
Metric Target Actual Notes
WAM 35 47 Ahead of target
30-day retention 70% 71% Roughly stable
60-day retention — 63% New metric; concerning gap vs. 30-day
Avg sessions/user/week 1.5 1.3 Below target
Referral rate (% of active users who’ve referred) — 68% Much higher than expected
NPS — +52 First measurement
--- ## Phase 3: v2.0 (In Progress — March–April 2026) ### What we’re building - Manager Insights Dashboard - Performance Review Drafting Assist - Redesigned session-start experience - Explicit privacy model in onboarding ### Hypotheses we’re testing 1. **Dashboard will increase days-per-week active.** If action item tracking is already a pull into the product, a dedicated action-item-focused home screen should increase open frequency. 2. **Performance review drafting will be a retention anchor.** The feature is explicitly designed to give users a moment of “this product saved me 4 hours” — the kind of experience that creates evangelism. 3. **One-click session start will reduce session-start abandonment.** We estimate 15–20% of “intended sessions” never start because the friction of navigating to the tool interrupts the flow. This is invisible in our current data. 4. **Explicit privacy framing will reduce early churn from skeptics.** The users who leave without explanation in weeks 1–2 may include people who had an unanswered privacy concern. Surfacing the model upfront should help. --- ## Cross-Phase Learnings (Patterns That Keep Showing Up) ### 1. The product is most valuable during moments of transition Every time users articulate a specific “this helped me,” it’s tied to a transition: a new hire joining, a performance review coming up, a direct report expressing they’re unhappy with their career growth. This suggests we should design for moments of transition more explicitly — not just steady-state support. ### 2. The first two weeks are make-or-break We’ve seen this in churn data and in qualitative interviews. Users who don’t form a note-taking habit in the first two weeks tend not to stay. The product’s value is time-delayed, and we haven’t solved the gap between “investing time” and “seeing return.” ### 3. The product changes behavior, not just workflow The finding we’re proudest of: users who stay report that their 1:1s have changed quality, not just their note-taking. They come more prepared, their reports feel more seen, and they follow through more. This is the outcome we’re after. It’s hard to measure directly, but it shows up consistently in qualitative feedback. ### 4. Positioning is doing real work “Built for the manager, not HR” is not just a tagline — it’s genuinely changing how prospects respond to cold outreach. When we reference this framing in initial messages, response rates are 2x higher than when we lead with feature descriptions. The positioning deserves continued investment. ### 5. Our best users are our salespeople The 30% of users who’ve referred someone are doing this because the product genuinely changed something for them. We’re not asking for referrals — they’re happening organically. This is the behavior we should be designing around and amplifying. --- ## Things We Wish We’d Known Earlier - **Privacy is a table-stakes concern, not an objection.** Build the privacy model into the product before you need to defend it. - **AI features need data before they need sophistication.** Don’t build the AI feature before there’s enough data to make it useful. It’s worse to have a mediocre AI feature visible than no AI feature at all. - **Churn in the first two weeks is a product problem, not a marketing problem.** Don’t try to fix it with better targeting. Fix it with a better early experience. - **The referral is the most meaningful signal of product-market fit you can observe.** Watch it earlier. --- *This document will be updated quarterly. Next update: June 2026.* "}

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"mission-vision-jtbd","url":"https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec814bbc67fe9d04b097ed","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec814bbc67fe9d04b097ed as of 2026-04-27T03:26:18.054Z: {"title":"mission-vision-jtbd"} # Acme — Mission, Vision & Jobs-to-Be-Done **Version:** 1.3 **Last Updated:** March 2026 **Owner:** Bryan Chen, CEO --- ## Mission To make engineering managers more effective at the thing that matters most — growing their people. --- ## Vision A world where every engineering manager has the coaching support, situational awareness, and decision-making clarity they need to run a high-performing team — without being buried in administrative overhead. We believe great engineering management is one of the highest-leverage forces in a technology company. When managers are effective, engineers grow faster, teams ship with fewer surprises, and organizations build cultures that attract and retain talent. When managers are ineffective — or simply overwhelmed — the entire organization absorbs the cost silently. Acme exists to tip that balance. --- ## The Problem Engineering managers at early-to-mid-stage startups (20–200 engineers) are being asked to do more than the role was ever designed to handle. They carry: - **People management** — 1:1s, performance feedback, career development, conflict resolution - **Project delivery** — sprint planning, cross-functional coordination, unblocking engineers - **Technical credibility** — staying close enough to the code to earn trust without becoming a bottleneck - **Administrative load** — hiring loops, calibrations, quarterly reviews, headcount planning The average EM in our target segment runs 18–24 meetings per week, manages 6–12 direct reports, and has no dedicated HR support. Their primary management tools are Notion, Google Docs, and their own memory. The result: the hardest part of the job — genuine coaching, career development, early detection of disengagement — consistently gets deprioritized. Not because managers don’t care, but because there’s no space left in the week. --- ## Jobs-to-Be-Done Framework We organize our product around three distinct jobs that engineering managers hire for: --- ### Job 1: The Building Job *“Help me run my team well day-to-day without drowning in process.”* **Trigger:** End of the sprint, upcoming 1:1, performance review cycle opening, new hire starting, team size crossing a threshold. **Desired outcome:** The manager shows up to interactions prepared, with the right context surfaced at the right time. They don’t feel like they’re winging it. **Pain today:**
- Scrambling to remember what was discussed in last week’s 1:1
- Copying notes from Slack/Notion/Linear into a performance doc
- Writing performance reviews that they feel aren’t accurate because they can’t recall 6 months of context
- Spending 30–45 min preparing for each 1:1 (or not preparing and feeling guilty) **How Acme addresses it:**
- Persistent, structured 1:1 note-taking with continuity across sessions
- Surfacing past commitments and action items before each meeting
- Automated signals from connected tools (PR velocity, ticket throughput, Slack patterns) to prompt coaching topics
- AI-drafted performance summaries built from real longitudinal data --- ### Job 2: The Selling Job *“Help me demonstrate that my team is performing well and that I’m a strong manager.”* **Trigger:** Approaching calibration cycles, preparing for skip-level conversations, justifying headcount, making a case for a direct report’s promotion. **Desired outcome:** The manager can walk into a calibration with confidence, backed by concrete examples, and advocate effectively for their team. **Pain today:**
- Can’t remember specific examples when writing performance reviews
- Has a gut sense that someone is ready for promotion but can’t articulate the evidence
- Calibrations feel like whoever tells the best story wins, not whoever has the best evidence
- Promotion docs take 4–6 hours to write and still feel thin **How Acme addresses it:**
- Promotion packet drafting from structured 1:1 history
- Achievement tagging with timestamps and impact framing
- Continuous “evidence collection” so calibration prep is low-effort instead of a fire drill --- ### Job 3: The Early Warning Job *“Help me catch problems before they become crises.”* **Trigger:** A usually engaged engineer goes quiet. A project starts slipping. Interpersonal tension is building. Someone’s performance is degrading but hasn’t crossed a threshold yet. **Desired outcome:** The manager sees the signal early enough to course-correct, rather than finding out during a resignation conversation. **Pain today:**
- Disengagement is often invisible until it’s too late
- No systematic way to track if 1:1s are actually having an impact
- Relies on gut feel and informal hallway conversations that don’t exist in remote/hybrid environments
- By the time a performance issue shows up in a formal review, it’s already 3 months old **How Acme addresses it:**
- Engagement trend analysis across 1:1 themes and participation signals
- Proactive nudges when patterns suggest someone may be at risk
- Side-by-side view of stated goals vs. actual progress across quarters --- ## Who We Build For **Primary persona: The Stretched EM**
- 2–5 years in the manager role
- Managing 6–10 engineers at a Series A–C startup
- No HR business partner; direct reports vary widely in seniority
- Technically strong but increasingly feeling like they’ve lost touch with the code
- Privately worried they’re not doing enough for their people **Secondary persona: The Scaling Lead**
- Engineering Lead or VP managing a growing org (10–30+ engineers across multiple teams)
- Concerned about consistency across managers they oversee
- Needs visibility without micromanaging
- Often promoted from individual contributor; management skills are self-taught --- ## Strategic Bets 1. **Integration over isolation.** EMs already live in Notion, Slack, Linear, GitHub, and Jira. Acme must meet them in their existing workflow — not ask them to move to a new workspace. 2. **Trust through longitudinal data.** The product becomes more valuable the longer it’s used. Our moat is the accumulated history of a manager’s team — something no competing tool can replicate without starting over. 3. **Manager-first, not HR-first.** We build for the person doing the work, not the compliance use case. Data stays under the manager’s control. No top-down surveillance design. 4. **Start narrow, expand outward.** The 1:1 is the highest-frequency, highest-leverage touchpoint in engineering management. We win there first, then expand to cover the full management lifecycle. --- ## North Star Metric **Weekly Active Managers (WAM):** The number of managers who interact meaningfully with Acme at least once per week (defined as opening a 1:1 session, reviewing an insight, or drafting/editing a note). Rationale: Weekly engagement is the minimum bar for a tool to be “in the workflow.” If we’re hitting this, the product has crossed the threshold from interesting to necessary. **Current:** 47 WAMs (as of March 2026) **Target (EOY 2026):** 300 WAMs --- ## What Success Looks Like in 18 Months - An EM tells us “I feel more prepared for conversations with my team than I ever have.” - A VP of Engineering says “I can see the health of my org in a way I couldn’t before.” - An engineer reports their 1:1s feel more focused on their actual career, not just project status updates. - A manager closes a promotion that they credit Acme with helping them build the case for. --- *“The best managers I’ve seen aren’t the ones who work the hardest. They’re the ones who have enough clarity to focus on the right things at the right time. That’s what we’re building.”*
— Bryan Chen, CEO "}

# Raw Interview Transcript
**Participant:** Nadia F. (pseudonym: Nadia Ferreira)
**Role:** Engineering Manager, Series A B2B SaaS (\~60 employees)
**Team size:** 6 direct reports
**Interview date:** December 3, 2025
**Interviewer:** Bryan Chen
**Duration:** 43 minutes
**Session type:** Round 2 — new prospect (no product experience)
**Transcript source:** Fireflies auto-transcription (unedited)
---
\[00:00:08\]
**Bryan:** Alright, we’re live. Nadia, thanks for doing this. Chris intro’d us and said you’d have a lot to say about this stuff.
\[00:00:15\]
**Nadia:** Yeah, he said you were building something for EMs and I was like, okay, I’ll talk. I always want to talk about this stuff. Nobody talks about it.
\[00:00:24\]
**Bryan:** What do you mean, nobody talks about it?
\[00:00:26\]
**Nadia:** Like, engineering management is — it’s a lonely job in a weird way. You’re between your team and leadership and you kind of absorb everything and you’re not supposed to complain. There’s not really a community for it the way there is for, like, engineering or design. So when someone wants to talk about it I’m there.
\[00:00:44\]
**Bryan:** I appreciate that. Let’s go there. Give me the picture of your life as an EM right now.
\[00:00:50\]
**Nadia:** Okay. So I’m at — I’ll say we’re Series A, about 60 people, we do B2B SaaS. I’ve been a manager for two years. I have six direct reports, four engineers and two data folks that kind of sit in my org for now. And the way I would describe my days is: I’m always in the middle of like four conversations at once and none of them are really resolved. Like someone needs a decision, someone needs feedback, someone needs me to go tell a product manager something on their behalf, and someone else needs me to actually do their performance review. All at the same time.
\[00:01:24\]
**Bryan:** How do you prioritize that?
\[00:01:27\]
**Nadia:** Whoever’s loudest. \[laughs\] No, I mean — mostly by urgency. But I’m very aware that the urgent stuff crowds out the important stuff. Like, my most important job is probably developing my people. And that’s the thing I do least intentionally. I do it, but I do it reactively. Someone tells me they want to grow in a certain direction and I say great and then two months pass and nothing happens.
\[00:01:55\]
**Bryan:** Tell me about that. The career development piece.
\[00:01:58\]
**Nadia:** So we don’t have a formal career ladder. Which means every career development conversation is essentially made up. I’m trying to tell someone what the path to senior engineer looks like at this company, and I’m partially inventing it as I go. And I feel like I’m not the right person to be doing that — I’m not a senior IC anymore, I don’t know if what I’m telling them is accurate. And so I get avoidant about it. Like, I’ll have a career conversation in a 1:1 and then I won’t bring it up again for three months because I don’t really know what I’m talking about.
\[00:02:29\]
**Bryan:** Does anyone on your team push back on that or notice?
\[00:02:33\]
**Nadia:** One person does. Kavya. She’s really driven and she will absolutely ask me “so what happened with that” and I have to have an answer. Which is good — it keeps me honest. But the other folks are more deferential and I think I rely on that too much. I don’t chase the conversation as hard with them because they’re not pushing.
\[00:02:54\]
**Bryan:** And are you worried about any of those folks?
\[00:02:57\]
**Nadia:** Yeah. I have one person — I’ll call him Dom — who’s been here 18 months and has never directly told me what he wants next. Like he’ll answer questions when I ask them but he doesn’t volunteer anything. And I don’t know if that’s fine — like maybe he’s happy and just wants to do good work — or if something’s brewing. I genuinely don’t know. And that ambiguity is uncomfortable.
\[00:03:22\]
**Bryan:** How do you try to surface that in 1:1s?
\[00:03:25\]
**Nadia:** I’ll ask open questions. Like “how are you feeling about work lately” or “what’s been most interesting to you.” And he’ll answer, but they’re short answers. And then I don’t know if I’m getting the real thing or the polite version. I’ve been a manager two years and I still can’t always tell.
\[00:03:44\]
**Bryan:** Fair. Let me ask you about 1:1s more specifically. Walk me through how you typically run them.
\[00:03:50\]
**Nadia:** So I have weekly 1:1s with everyone, 30 minutes. I have a shared doc with each person — Google Doc — where we both add topics before the meeting. That part works okay. The doc is the agenda. What doesn’t work is the continuity. Like, after each meeting, I’ll sometimes add notes at the bottom of the doc, but it’s not consistent. Maybe I do it 60% of the time. And then a month later I’m scrolling up through this doc trying to find what we talked about and it’s this big wall of unstructured text and it’s not actually useful.
\[00:04:23\]
**Bryan:** What do you do when you can’t find what you need?
\[00:04:26\]
**Nadia:** I ask them. Which is embarrassing. I’ll say something like “remind me where we landed on that.” And they know. They know you don’t remember.
\[00:04:35\]
**Bryan:** Does it matter? Like does that dynamic have a cost?
\[00:04:39\]
**Nadia:** I think so. It sends a signal. Even if they’re gracious about it, you can tell they notice. And for the people who are more junior and looking to me for guidance and structure, I think it undermines trust a little bit. Like, if you can’t remember what I told you three weeks ago, how seriously were you taking it?
\[00:04:58\]
**Bryan:** That’s a good way to put it. What about action items? Things you commit to in a 1:1?
\[00:05:04\]
**Nadia:** \[pause\] Honestly I’m bad at this. I’ll say “I’ll look into that” and then it lives in my head and sometimes it falls out. I don’t have a system for tracking manager action items. My system is like — the important ones I’ll put in my personal Notion. The less important ones I’ll remember, or not remember. It’s not great.
\[00:05:24\]
**Bryan:** How often do you drop something?
\[00:05:27\]
**Nadia:** More than I want to admit. Maybe once a week something slips that I said I’d do. Usually small things. But small things accumulate.
\[00:05:37\]
**Bryan:** Tell me about your last performance review cycle.
\[00:05:41\]
**Nadia:** Oh god. Okay. So we just did one in October. It was my second cycle as a manager. And the way it works at our company is you write a self-assessment, your manager writes an assessment, and then there’s a calibration. And I’m writing assessments for six people and I have — I have nothing. Like, I have the Google Docs with the half-updated notes, and I have my memory. That’s it. So I’m writing in Notion, I’m trying to reconstruct the quarter, and I’m thinking, okay what did Kavya do this quarter. And I remember the big launch in August, and I remember a conversation we had in September about something — but I can’t remember what. And I remember she had some tension with someone from product. But that’s kind of it. And then I have to write like four paragraphs that accurately represents her contribution for three months. And I feel like I’m writing fiction. Like I’m writing a plausible story, not a true story.
\[00:06:36\]
**Bryan:** How long does each review take you?
\[00:06:38\]
**Nadia:** Like three hours. Per person. Which is — yeah. Eighteen hours of review writing in a cycle, basically. And I still feel like the output is not good.
\[00:06:49\]
**Bryan:** What would “good” look like to you?
\[00:06:52\]
**Nadia:** Good would be — I could pull up something that told me, here are five meaningful things Kavya said she was working on this quarter, and here’s what actually happened with each of them. With dates. So when I write “she owned the migration project and delivered it on time” I actually know that’s true because I tracked it, not because I kind of remember it. And the more specific stuff too — like the moments where someone showed up in a way that mattered. Those are the examples that make a performance review real. And right now those examples just evaporate.
\[00:07:25\]
**Bryan:** Yeah. Okay — I want to share something with you briefly and get your reaction. Is that okay?
\[00:07:30\]
**Nadia:** Yeah, go ahead.
\[00:07:32\]
**Bryan:** So we’re building a tool for engineering managers. The core thing it does: it maintains a persistent, structured record of your 1:1 conversations — so you always have history when you sit down with someone, you can see what action items are open, and you get a starting point for performance reviews that’s based on what you actually said and tracked throughout the quarter. Not a finished review — a starting point. What’s your honest first reaction to that?
\[00:07:56\]
**Nadia:** \[pause\] Honestly my first reaction is — why doesn’t this exist already. Like this seems really obvious. The thing I’m doing right now — the scattered Google Docs, the Slack search — that’s insane. It shouldn’t be that hard to have a structured record of conversations I’m having every week.
\[00:08:16\]
**Bryan:** What would make you not try it?
\[00:08:19\]
**Nadia:** Friction. If there’s setup, I won’t do it. If I have to import things, configure things, connect things — I’ll start and I’ll stop. I need something that works the first time I open it. Like literally the first 1:1 I use it for should feel better than not using it. If the first session is me setting things up, I’m out.
\[00:08:41\]
**Bryan:** What else?
\[00:08:43\]
**Nadia:** I’d want to know who can see it. I’m going to be honest in there about my concerns about people on my team. Like “Dom is worrying me and I don’t know why.” I don’t want my CEO to see that. Or my reports to see it. I need to know it’s mine.
\[00:08:59\]
**Bryan:** Yeah, that’s come up a lot. What would it take to trust that?
\[00:09:04\]
**Nadia:** I mean, just tell me clearly. Don’t bury it. Like if you say upfront “this is private, your employer can’t access it, your reports can’t see it” — that’s enough. I don’t need to audit your security infrastructure. I just need to know you’ve thought about it and you’ve made a choice, and you’re telling me what the choice is.
\[00:09:22\]
**Bryan:** Okay. Is there anything about the concept that seems off or that you’d push back on?
\[00:09:28\]
**Nadia:** The AI part, potentially. Like if it’s summarizing my notes or generating suggestions — what’s the quality of that going to be? Because if it’s bad it’s actively misleading. I’d rather have a blank page than a confidently wrong suggestion.
\[00:09:44\]
**Bryan:** What would good look like? For the AI piece specifically.
\[00:09:48\]
**Nadia:** Specific. If it’s telling me I have an open action item with Kavya about the career ladder conversation from three weeks ago — I find that credible because it’s just reading my own notes back to me. If it’s saying “consider asking about team morale” — that’s useless. That could apply to anyone. The specificity is what makes it feel like it knows my situation vs. just being generic AI stuff.
\[00:10:10\]
**Bryan:** Got it. Last few questions. You mentioned this is a lonely job. How do you deal with that?
\[00:10:17\]
**Nadia:** I talk to other EMs when I can. There’s a Slack community I’m in — Rands Leadership Slack, do you know it? — and I lurk there a lot. Occasionally post. It helps to know other people are dealing with the same stuff.
\[00:10:30\]
**Bryan:** Is there anyone specific in your network you think I should talk to?
\[00:10:34\]
**Nadia:** Yeah, there’s an EM at a healthtech company — her name’s Dara, she manages a team of like 14 and has been doing it for five years. She’d have a totally different perspective than me because she’s got a much bigger team and they do have HR support. Might be interesting contrast.
\[00:10:50\]
**Bryan:** I’d love that. Okay, one last thing — you work at a company with no formal career ladder, and you mentioned kind of making it up. If we were building something to help with that part specifically — the career development piece — what would you want?
\[00:11:06\]
**Nadia:** \[pause\] Honestly I want a framework. Like just — this is what a senior engineer looks like at a company like yours, these are the behaviors and the evidence you’re looking for. I could adapt it. I’m not expecting a one-size-fits-all answer, but I need a starting point. Because right now I’m making that up from scratch too and it’s — it’s not good. I’m probably giving different answers to different people on my team.
\[00:11:32\]
**Bryan:** Interesting. And would you want that to be connected to your actual notes, or more like a standalone resource?
\[00:11:38\]
**Nadia:** Connected, definitely. Like — here’s the framework, and here’s what I’ve actually documented about Kavya that maps to it. Or gaps in the documentation. That would be amazing. That would actually help me have the career conversations I’m currently avoiding.
\[00:11:55\]
**Bryan:** Okay. This has been really great. I really appreciate it.
\[00:12:00\]
**Nadia:** Yeah for sure. Can you let me know when the thing exists? I would try it.
\[00:12:05\]
**Bryan:** Absolutely. I’ll send you a link when we’re ready.
\[00:12:08\]
**Nadia:** Cool. Good luck with it.
\[00:12:10\]
**Bryan:** Thanks Nadia.

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"interview-guide-v2","url":"https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec81b79401ee3537616b25","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec81b79401ee3537616b25 as of 2026-04-27T03:26:23.444Z: {"title":"interview-guide-v2"} # Acme — User Interview Guide v2.0 **Created:** December 2025 **Replaces:** v1.0 (see interview-guide-v1.md for retrospective notes) **Used for:** Rounds 3+ (mixed: new prospects + existing users) **Status:** Current **Owner:** Sarah Kim, Head of Product --- ## Purpose This guide is designed for two session types:
- **Prospect sessions:** EMs who don’t use Acme. Focus on problem depth and behavioral mapping.
- **User sessions:** Active Acme users. Focus on where we’re delivering value, where we’re failing, and what’s next. Flag which type this is at the top of your notes. --- ## Pre-Interview Checklist - [ ] LinkedIn review — understand their background, company stage, approximate team size - [ ] For user sessions: pull Acme usage data (WAM, feature engagement, last active date) - [ ] Write 3 hypotheses you want to test in this specific session (don’t skip this) - [ ] Confirm Fireflies is connected to the meeting link - [ ] Have Notion interview log open to take live notes --- ## Intro (2 min) “Thanks for making time. I want to get the most out of this for both of us, so I’ll be mostly asking questions and listening today — I’m not pitching anything. We’ll have a chance at the end for you to ask me stuff. Quick housekeeping: I’d like to record this for my own notes — transcription only, not shared externally. Is that okay? Alright, let’s jump in.” --- ## Part 1: Grounding (5 min) The goal here is not to fill out a screener — it’s to understand their specific context so you can ask better questions for the rest of the session. 1. “Paint me a picture of your current setup. How many people are you managing right now, and what’s the company look like?” 2. “In the last two weeks — just roughly — where did most of your time actually go?” *Listen for: ratio of people work to project work to technical work. Note what they volunteer vs. what they omit.* 3. “Do you have any dedicated HR support, or is it pretty much on you?” --- ## Part 2: A Specific Moment (10 min) This section replaces the abstract “how do you run 1:1s” questions from v1. We anchor everything to a specific recent experience. 1. “Tell me about a conversation you had with one of your reports in the last few weeks that you felt good about afterward. What made it work?” 2. “Now tell me about one that didn’t go the way you wanted — or that you weren’t as prepared for as you would have liked.” *Probe:* “What would you have needed to have in front of you to show up better to that conversation?” 3. “When was the last time you felt like you caught a problem with someone on your team early enough to actually fix it? What was the signal you noticed?” 4. “On the flip side — has there ever been a time you found out something was wrong later than you would have liked? What happened there?” *Listen for: early warning signals, what data they do/don’t have access to, the cost of latency.* --- ## Part 3: Performance & Development (10 min) 1. “Think about the last performance review cycle you went through. Walk me through it — start to finish, from when you first realized it was coming to when you submitted the forms.” *Don’t interrupt. Let them describe the whole thing. Note the pain points they volunteer.* *Follow up:* “How long did that take you, roughly?” *Follow up:* “How did you feel about the output when you were done?” 2. “Was there anyone on your team who you felt you wrote a particularly strong review for? What made it strong?” 3. “Was there anyone you felt like you underserved in that process? Why?” 4. “What would a ‘perfect’ performance review process look like for you? Not the company’s version — yours.” --- ## Part 4: Current Tools & Workarounds (8 min) *Don’t ask about their tool stack in the abstract. Ask in the context of specific moments from Part 2 and 3.* 1. “When you were prepping for that 1:1 you mentioned — what did you actually pull up? What were you working from?” 2. “For the performance reviews — what were your sources? Where did the content come from?” 3. “Do you use anything specifically for tracking notes on your direct reports over time? What does that look like?” *If they say Notion/Google Docs:* “Can you show me what that looks like? Even just a quick screenshare?” *If they have nothing:* “How do you not lose context from quarter to quarter?” 4. “What’s the biggest gap in what you have access to today?” --- ## Part 5A: Existing User Deep Dive (12 min) *\[For user sessions only — skip to 5B for prospects\]* 1. “Tell me where Acme has actually shown up in your workflow. I don’t want the highlight reel — I want to know what you genuinely use and what you ignore.” 2. “What’s the moment you felt like Acme was most useful? What was the context?” 3. “What’s a situation where you reached for Acme and it didn’t quite deliver — or where you chose not to use it even though it theoretically should have applied?” 4. “If you had to describe what Acme does for you in one sentence — to a peer, not to a recruiter — what would you say?” 5. “Is there something you wish Acme did that it doesn’t? Or something you wish it did differently?” --- ## Part 5B: Prospect Concept Test (5 min) *\[For prospect sessions only — skip if user session\]* “Quick context on us: we’re building a tool for engineering managers. The core job it does: it lives in your management workflow — 1:1s, performance reviews, career development conversations — and it helps you have the context you need for those conversations, without spending hours digging up notes and writing things from scratch. Think of it as the organized, attentive version of yourself that you don’t have bandwidth to be. What’s your honest first reaction to that?” *Follow up:*
- “What part of that lands most?”
- “What’s the most skeptical thought you had just now?”
- “What would you need to see to take it seriously?” --- ## Close (3 min) “That’s really helpful. A couple of last things. Is there anything I should have asked that I didn’t?” “Who else in your network do you think is dealing with this stuff and might have interesting things to say? If you’re comfortable, I’d love a warm intro.” *(If user session)* “Is there anything from this conversation you’d like us to specifically follow up on — like we said we were going to do X and you want to make sure we actually do it?” --- ## Post-Interview Protocol **Within 2 hours:**
- \[ \] Send thank-you email (include offer to share findings if they’re interested)
- \[ \] Log referrals in CRM **Within 24 hours:**
- \[ \] Write raw impressions in Notion — use the `## Raw Impressions` template
- \[ \] Pull 3–5 verbatim quotes worth archiving
- \[ \] Note your 3 pre-session hypotheses and rate: confirmed / partially confirmed / disconfirmed / unclear **Within 48 hours:**
- \[ \] Code the interview in the research database
- \[ \] Flag any items that should go to the roadmap Slack channel immediately (don’t wait for synthesis) --- ## Facilitation Tips **On silence:** Let it sit. EMs are thoughtful people. If they pause after a question, don’t fill the gap. The most interesting things usually come after 3–5 seconds of silence. **On leading:** If you catch yourself completing their sentences or suggesting answers, stop. Rephrase with “What was that like for you?” and let them drive. **On features:** If they start asking about specific features or requesting things, redirect: “That’s useful to know — before we get into product specifics, I want to make sure I understand the underlying problem well. Can you tell me more about what you’d be trying to accomplish with that?” **On screenshares:** Always ask. Most people say yes. A 2-minute screenshare of their actual Notion setup is worth 20 minutes of description. "}

## Scope
Transcript evidence and prior learnings used for April 2026 retention synthesis.
## Research question
Why is career growth feature retention low, what repeat-use barrier matters most, and what behavior change seems most promising?
## Participant set
- Nadia F. — Series A, 6 reports, newer manager, prospect, strong stated career-growth pain
- Patrick M. — Series B, 12 reports, active user, repeat-use behavior visible
- Tyler R. — Series A, 9 reports, active user, repeat-use behavior visible
## Code book
- `career_conv_unstructured` — manager lacks formal structure for career conversations
- `needs_framework` — explicit request for framework/rubric
- `avoidance_after_initial_conv` — career topic raised once, then deferred
- `low_repeat_cadence` — natural cadence of problem is infrequent
- `needs_notes_connected_guidance` — guidance must connect to report-specific notes/evidence
- `behavior_change_prompt` — tool can change follow-through behavior
- `setup_friction_kills_adoption` — setup/onboarding suppresses use
- `needs_immediate_value` — first-use payoff is required
- `data_density_drives_quality` — feature quality depends on note history
- `rich_get_richer_usage` — active users get more value; less-active users get less
- `workflow_friction_limits_breadth` — interaction overhead narrows use cases/coverage
- `repeat_use_requires_low_friction` — habit depends on near-zero friction
- `weekly_feature_misaligned_with_daily_job` — cadence mismatch between feature and actual work
- `needs_between_session_capture` — evidence capture needed outside scheduled 1:1s
- `delayed_value` — payoff is time-delayed
- `investment_before_return` — user contributes before receiving value
- `usage_concentrates_on_high_stakes_people` — product reused mostly for a subset of reports
- `not_universal_habit` — use does not become a consistent habit across all reports
- `high_value_output_anchor` — strongest pull is a valuable output artifact
- `workflow_outcome_pull` — repeat use happens when feature helps complete a consequential task
## Coded excerpts
### Nadia F.
1. “every career development conversation is essentially made up”  
Codes: `career_conv_unstructured`, `needs_framework`
1. “I get avoidant about it… I won’t bring it up again for three months”  
Codes: `avoidance_after_initial_conv`, `low_repeat_cadence`
1. “I want a framework… I need a starting point”  
Codes: `needs_framework`
1. “Connected, definitely… here’s what I’ve actually documented about Kavya that maps to it”  
Codes: `needs_notes_connected_guidance`, `behavior_change_prompt`
1. “If there’s setup, I won’t do it… the first 1:1… should feel better than not using it”  
Codes: `setup_friction_kills_adoption`, `needs_immediate_value`
### Patrick M.
1. “the people I use it most for, the suggestions are better… the people I use it less for, the suggestions are worse”  
Codes: `data_density_drives_quality`, `rich_get_richer_usage`
1. “If it was one click to open and start, I’d do it for everyone”  
Codes: `workflow_friction_limits_breadth`, `repeat_use_requires_low_friction`
1. “management is a daily thing”  
Codes: `weekly_feature_misaligned_with_daily_job`, `needs_between_session_capture`
1. “I would use \[performance draft\] every single cycle”  
Codes: `high_value_output_anchor`, `workflow_outcome_pull`
### Tyler R.
1. “the first couple weeks were… I was building a database… payoff… came week three”  
Codes: `delayed_value`, `investment_before_return`
1. “for my senior folks… I don’t always remember to open it”  
Codes: `usage_concentrates_on_high_stakes_people`, `not_universal_habit`
1. “what if… a button that said ‘draft a summary’… I would use that every single time”  
Codes: `high_value_output_anchor`, `workflow_outcome_pull`
## Breadth, depth, segments, contradictions
- **Breadth:** career-growth pain appears across prior synthesis and one transcript directly; repeat-use dynamics are evidenced more strongly in two active-user transcripts.
- **Depth:** direct transcript depth is strongest for delayed value, workflow friction, and output-driven reuse; direct feature-level career-retention depth is limited.
- **Segments:** newer managers ask for frameworks; larger-team managers emphasize friction reduction and output creation; usage concentrates around high-stakes reports.
- **Contradictions:** users say career development matters a lot, but active repeated behavior centers on continuity, action items, and performance-review prep.
- **Say/do gap:** stated desire for career help does not automatically translate into repeated use of a standalone career-growth workflow.
## Theme clusters
1. Career growth pain is real but low-frequency.
2. Delayed value and setup friction suppress repeat use.
3. Generic guidance is weak; evidence-linked help is stronger.
4. Best opportunity is prompting follow-up on real growth threads inside existing workflows.
## Notes on defensibility
- This is a constrained evidence base with only 3 available transcripts in Notion.
- No feature-specific analytics or dedicated career-growth PRD were found.
- Use this as directional evidence for hypothesis generation, not a causal feature-retention postmortem.

{"metadata":{"type":"page"},"title":"retention-synthesis-career-growth-next-build-Apr-2026","url":"https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec810199ddd02c431566ed","text":"Here is the result of "view" for the Page with URL https://www.notion.so/34f9952098ec810199ddd02c431566ed as of 2026-04-27T06:02:00.250Z: {"title":"retention-synthesis-career-growth-next-build-Apr-2026"} ## Research question and scope **Question:** Why is career growth feature retention low, what repeat-use barrier matters most, and what behavior change seems most promising? **Scope:** Smallest defensible synthesis using existing Notion product context, prior synthesis, and available transcript evidence. **Sources reviewed:** - `mission-vision-jtbd` - `user-research-methodology` - `interview-guide-v1` - `interview-synthesis-round1` - `interview-synthesis-round2` - `career-growth-retention-coding-notes-Apr-2026` - Raw transcripts: `raw-transcript-nadia-f`, `raw-transcript-patrick-m`, `raw-transcript-tyler-r` **Participant set used in evidence base:** - Nadia F. — Series A, 6 reports, newer manager, prospect, strong stated career-growth pain - Patrick M. — Series B, 12 reports, active user, repeat-use behavior visible - Tyler R. — Series A, 9 reports, active user, repeat-use behavior visible **Important limitation:** Notion workspace did **not** surface a dedicated career-growth feature PRD, launch retrospective, feature analytics page, or a larger feature-specific transcript set. This synthesis therefore explains likely retention barriers using adjacent evidence from career-development needs and observed repeat-use behavior in the product. It is directional for next-build hypotheses, not a direct causal postmortem. --- ## Product context most relevant to this question - Career development is explicitly in Acme’s core JTBD, but the product strategy says to **start narrow with the 1:1** because that is the highest-frequency management workflow. - Round 1 found career development is **high-anxiety, low-frequency**, especially for newer managers. - Round 2 explicitly marked career development as **still theoretical** and recommended validating it with active users before increasing investment. - Prior retention learning in Round 2: value is vulnerable in weeks 1–2 when users are investing before payoff, and friction at session start suppresses habit formation. --- ## Observations (evidence, not interpretation)
Participant Observation Codes
Nadia F. “every career development conversation is essentially made up” `career_conv_unstructured`, `needs_framework`
Nadia F. “I get avoidant about it… I’ll have a career conversation in a 1:1 and then I won’t bring it up again for three months” `avoidance_after_initial_conv`, `low_repeat_cadence`
